Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a comprehensive "33% Rule" for ad creative sourcing (balancing AI, UGC armies, and in-house content) and outlines how to map creative formats to the customer's stage of awareness to prevent ad fatigue and scale Meta campaigns. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Establishing the "33% Rule" for creative production volume: sourcing 33% of ads from AI tools (for rapid, low-cost angle testing), 33% from a "UGC Army" (leveraging TikTok influencer seeding to generate thousands of authentic videos), and 33% from in-house content (founder stories and behind-the-scenes footage to build deep trust). Implementing the "Creative Flywheel," where winning UGC concepts (e.g., an unexpected focus on simple ingredient labels) inform the creation of new in-house and AI-generated statics, creating a perpetual cycle of fresh creatives to feed Meta's Andromeda algorithm. messaging and positioning / Structuring ad creatives based on the buyer's stage of awareness (Unaware, Problem Aware, Solution Aware, Product Aware, and Most Aware) and placing them all within the same ad set to allow Meta's algorithm to serve the right message at the right time. Transitioning from the outdated "2026 Strategy" (finding one winning format and only creating minor visual variants, which leads to rapid fatigue) to the "2027 Strategy" (maintaining 10-15 completely distinct formats and angles simultaneously). Scaling campaigns through "personification," which involves expanding the target market by addressing entirely different avatars (e.g., pivoting a sleep supplement ad from targeting "people who struggle to fall asleep" to "people who wake up groggy").

Look for. The definition of the "33% Rule" for ad creative: splitting creative production equally across AI-generated content (for rapid testing), UGC armies (for high volume and authenticity), and in-house content (for deep brand trust). The reason the old strategy of making minor visual variants of a single winning ad fails: all ad spend gets stuck on one specific format, causing rapid creative fatigue and a subsequent crash in ROAS. The definition of "personification" in ad scaling: creating distinct ads tailored to completely different customer avatars and specific use cases (e.g., an athlete vs. a busy professional) to unlock new audience pockets once the primary avatar is exhausted.
Skip. Generic lists of third-party influencer seeding tools (e.g., Tribe, Yuko) without specific implementation methodologies attached.
